One planting yields cut-and-come-again leaves for years, with the calendar pausing only where the summer is genuinely too hot for a cool-preferring plant. Windows are modeled from chives' cold-hardy, cool-season envelope and the regional planting-calendar sources. (UMN; Wisconsin Horticulture; MSU)

Constant moisture and steady feeding through the long season are the limiting factors, not heat.

value.chill_basis_seasoned: Mid-Atlantic winters bank abundant, reliable chill accumulation: NC State Extension puts the statewide floor at over 1,000 chilling hours a year, and a wider four-source check (NC State, Penn State, Virginia Cooperative Extension, University of Maryland Extension) confirms the belt delivers roughly 1,000 to 1,350 hours on the warmer Coastal Plain (zone 8) and 1,100 to 1,500 hours in the cooler Piedmont interior (zone 7). 7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7's winter lows sit at this crop's cold edge: standard pomegranate wood can be damaged or killed back in a hard freeze, so cold-hardy cultivars (Salavatski, Kazake) on a warm, sheltered, hot-summer site are the reliable path, and even those crop best in a mild winter followed by a hot summer. Chill is never the issue (the crop needs only about 100 hours); winter cold and this belt's own summer humidity both cap the crop below fully reliable.

A cold-hardy cultivar on a warm, sheltered, well-drained site is the reliable path if you want to grow it here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder Coastal Plain and Tidewater zone sits close to the edge for the hardiest lemon option: Improved Meyer, a lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F and is documented surviving the milder half of zone 8 with protection. A container Meyer brought under cover, or fully indoors, on hard-freeze nights can persist here for years, but this zone's colder pockets and periodic harder freezes still reach past that threshold, so there is no dependable in-ground or even reliably fruiting container crop, only a protected specimen that may bloom in milder winters. True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more tender still and does not belong outdoors here at all.
8.suitability_note_beginner: This is about as good as lemon gets here: Improved Meyer, the cold-hardy lemon type, can survive in the milder Tidewater pockets of this zone for years if you bring it under cover, or fully indoors, on the coldest nights. It still is not a plant you leave outside all winter, and do not expect a reliable crop of fruit. Regular lemon types are too tender to try here at all.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Improved Meyer's own documented cold limit, the low-to-mid 20s°F, sits right at this zone's milder Tidewater edge; the zone's colder pockets and any harder freeze still exceed it, so container culture with real winter protection is the honest baseline, not a dependable outdoor planting.

Model: Utah / modified-Weinberger chill hours, accumulated hours with temperature between 32 and 45 degrees F over the winter dormant season (the model the cited extensions use and the definition carried in this dataset's chill prose). One crop-invariant winter-chill-DELIVERED band per region+zone, reconciled to published T1 extension chill-accumulation data, NEVER derived from the USDA winter-low zone. Sources by region: northern_tier / ca_interior reconciled to UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center chill-accumulation data (ucd_fruitnut); ca_north_coast / ca_south_coast / ca_desert to UC ANR and UC Statewide IPM California chill data (ucanr_ext, uc_ipm); se_gulf to University of Georgia Cooperative Extension chill-hour station data (uga_ext); warm_arid to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Texas chill-hour maps and University of Arizona Cooperative Extension elevation chill bands (tamu_agrilife, uarizona_ext); low_desert_az to University of Arizona Cooperative Extension low-desert chill data (uarizona_ext); fl_peninsula / hawaii_tropical to UF/IFAS Extension low-chill and near-zero-chill data (uf_ifas_hs1153). rgv (2026-07-13, RGV / subtropical-South-Texas region arc, zones 9-10) reconciled to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension South Texas / Lower Rio Grande Valley chill-hour guidance (tamu_agrilife): AgriLife Extension horticulturist Larry Stein places Rio Grande Valley orchard chill requirements at roughly 200 to 300 chill hours, and the Valley's subtropical, near-frost-free winters (about 340 frost-free days) bank essentially no chill in warm winters, so the delivered band is [0, 300] for both zone 9 and zone 10, corroborated by LSU AgCenter's 200 to 300 chill-hour figure for the comparably subtropical coastal-south-Louisiana Gulf climate (lsu_agcenter); RGV sits just above the deep-tropical fl_peninsula z11 / hawaii_tropical [0, 150] floor and below the se_gulf band, and the 0 low edge (warm winters bank near-zero chill) is what drives the A3 no-fruit split for temperate stone and pome fruit. Bands are the climate's typical winter delivery envelope, widened across zones where station data and crop-author estimates differ; per-variety chill-REQUIRED (chill_hours_required / chill_hours_range) is the separate axis and is unchanged. pnw (2026-07-14, maritime Pacific Northwest region arc, Task 3, zones 8-9) reconciled to WSU Skagit County Extension / WSU Mount Vernon NWREC: Skagit Valley AWN (Agricultural Weather Network) station data, 2007-2015, banks 968 to 1950 chill hours annually (average ~1468) -- Hunter, 'The Importance of Chilling,' WSU Skagit County Extension, 2016.
